$schema: Plain-language mythology glossary. term + pronunciation + plain explanation + optional source note. Surfaced in the Glossary panel and linked from creature/story text.

entries.meaning: The fairy folk of Ireland — 'the people of the mounds'. Often linked to the Tuatha Dé Danann, who were said to withdraw into the hills.
entries.note: Also written aes sídhe. Singular dwelling: a sídhe (shee).

entries.meaning: A fairy mound or hill — frequently a real neolithic passage tomb — understood as a doorway to the Otherworld.
entries.note: Newgrange (Brú na Bóinne) is the most famous such mound.

entries.meaning: The red feathered cap a Merrow wears to travel beneath the waves. Without it she cannot return to the sea.
entries.note: Recorded by Thomas Crofton Croker in the 1820s.

entries.meaning: Seal-folk who shed their skin to take human form. The hidden-sealskin motif is shared across Ireland, Scotland and the Northern Isles.
A shapeshifting spirit, by turns helpful and mischievous. Gives its name to Puck in English folklore.
entries.note: The month of November is Mí na Samhna; the Púca claims the hedgerow fruit after Samhain.

entries.meaning: The 'Land of the Young' — an Otherworld realm of endless youth and plenty, reached over or under the western sea.
entries.note: Home of Niamh, who took Oisín there in the Fenian Cycle.

entries.meaning: The festival marking the end of harvest and the dark half of the year, when the veil between worlds was thinnest.
entries.note: Falls around 1 November; an ancestor of Halloween.

entries.meaning: 'The Cattle Raid of Cooley' — the central epic of the Ulster Cycle, in which Queen Medb of Connacht invades Ulster to seize a prize bull.
entries.note: Survives in the 12th-century Book of Leinster and earlier sources.

entries.meaning: 'The folk of the goddess Danu' — a divine race who ruled Ireland before the Milesians, later remembered as the Aos Sí.
entries.note: Their stories fill the Mythological Cycle.

entries.meaning: A goddess of fate, war and sovereignty. Her raven companions perch at the threshold between the living and the dead, witnessing all.
entries.note: Often appears as a triple goddess: Badb, Macha and Nemain.

entries.meaning: Lord of the sea and guardian of the Otherworld. He rides the waves on a chariot and lends his name to the Isle of Man.
entries.note: The selkie Branna dwells at the edge of his realm.

entries.meaning: 'Bright fire' — the Irish name for the will-o'-wisp. A cold, wandering flame seen over bogs and marshes after dark.
entries.note: Believed to be the breath of forgotten places or the souls of unbaptised children.

entries.meaning: The realm beyond the visible world — reached through fairy mounds, across the sea, or at liminal moments. Neither heaven nor hell, but parallel to the living world.
entries.note: Called Tír na nÓg, Mag Mell, Tír Tairngire and many other names depending on the tale.
